narrative.overview: Jarvis OS feels like a private systems console that happens to be conversational: dark enough for sustained desktop use, restrained enough that real evidence remains the visual focus, and precise enough that state, provenance, and permission boundaries are immediately legible. Cyan marks system energy and interaction, while green, amber, red, violet, and blue carry specific operational meaning rather than decorative variety. The interface is dense but not cryptic. Thin boundaries, tonal surface changes, compact controls, real lists, and measured motion communicate hierarchy without turning every datum into a card. The shared shell remains recognizable across full pages and temporary workspaces; route-specific compositions such as the /chat twin wings stay in their surface brief instead of becoming universal page templates.
keyCharacteristics: Near-black canvases with quiet, stepped surfaces.
Evidence-first lists and inspectors rather than summary decoration.
Cyan for system energy and primary interaction, with semantic status colors kept literal.
Workhorse sans typography for reading and mono only for measurements, identifiers, and machine state.
Fine borders and tonal layering before ambient shadow.
Responsive task continuity: desktop density collapses into rails, drawers, and focused mobile surfaces.

rules.name: The Cyan Has a Job Rule
rules.body: Cyan identifies system energy, focus, or a meaningful action; it is not a general decoration color.

rules.name: The Status Is Literal Rule
rules.body: Green means ready or complete, amber means pending or degraded, and red means error or blocked. Never swap them for visual variety.

rules.name: The Readable Before Compact Rule
rules.body: Functional labels and explanatory text remain readable at the real breakpoint; density is created through spacing and hierarchy, not sub-legible type.

rules.name: The Mono Means Machine Rule
rules.body: Use mono only when the content is measured, coded, timed, versioned, or machine-generated.

rules.name: The Center Owns Continuity Rule
rules.body: When a surface has a primary working object—conversation, inspector, document, or timeline—it retains readable width before supporting regions do.

rules.name: The Tonal Before Shadow Rule
rules.body: Add a new surface level with color and a fine boundary before adding a shadow. A shadow must describe real elevation or interaction state.

rules.name: The Radius Follows Scale Rule
rules.body: Small controls stay compact, panels stay gently rounded, and shell-level surfaces receive the largest radius. Do not apply one universal radius everywhere.

dos: Do make data provenance, readiness, selection, and approval boundaries visible beside the content they affect.
Do use real lists, previews, empty states, and recovery actions instead of decorative metrics.
Do preserve keyboard focus, readable labels, and task state when a desktop region becomes a rail or mobile drawer.
Do let a single semantic tone identify a temporary panel while the global cyan voice remains reserved for system interaction.
Do keep meaningful actions synchronized with the user's current task and keep low-level filtering local.
donts: Don't use cyan, green, amber, or red interchangeably for visual variety.
Don't promote every piece of content into a same-size card; use lists, inspectors, and open working space.
Don't use mono for ordinary prose or decorative technical styling.
Don't let temporary UI state masquerade as persisted domain truth or bypass approval boundaries.
Don't inherit legacy sub-10px functional labels or eyebrow/kicker patterns as new system primitives; they are existing debt, not the quality bar.
